text: Severin Roesen painted abundant fruit and flower still lifes, and is recognized today as one of the major American painters in that genre in the nineteenth century. He came from Boppard on the Rhine. Little is known about his early life and education. He married in 1847 and worked as a porcelain painter in Cologne. He lived from about 1815 to about 1872.

Alphonse Osbert studied at the École des Beaux-Arts, and his earliest passion was for the great Spanish masters, particularly Ribera. In the late 1880s his academic style shifted under the influence of acquaintances tied to Post-Impressionism and Symbolism. He gave up naturalistic painting for a Pointillist technique like that of Seurat and Signac. Puvis de Chavannes and the Symbolists inspired him too. He lived from 1857 to 1939.

The nickname Pesellino comes from the name of Francesco Pesellino's grandfather, the painter Giuliano Pesello. After his father Stefano di Francesco died in 1427, the boy went to live with his grandfather and became his pupil. He stayed in that studio until the grandfather's death. Then he formed working partnerships with other artists, such as Zanobi Strozzi and Fra Filippo Lippi. He was active in Florence and died in 1457.

Houbraken says Francisque Millet's father was a French ivory worker from Dijon who moved to Antwerp, where he found a market for his ivory work. When his son showed talent for drawing, he apprenticed him to Laurentius Frank, a cousin of Abraham Genoels. Millet painted Baroque landscapes. He came from Antwerp and died in Paris in 1679. He is also known as Jean-François Milée.

Jan van Noordt came from Schagen in North Holland, one of four sons of a schoolteacher and carillonneur. The family moved to Amsterdam in the late 1630s. His brothers Jacobus and Anthonie became the most prominent organists in the city, with posts in churches such as the Oude Kerk. Jan seems to have started training in Amsterdam well before 1640. He was a Dutch Golden Age painter.

Wilhelm von Wright's ancestors included Scottish merchants who settled in Narva in the 17th century. He grew up in Haminalahti, Kuopio, where his father, a retired major, owned the family estate. Two of his brothers, Magnus and Ferdinand, also became painters and illustrators. At Magnus's invitation he went to Sweden in 1823 and took part in making a multi-volume work on Swedish birds. He worked as an amateur naturalist too.

Bartolomeo Montagna is most famous for his many Madonnas, and his soft figures and eccentric marble architecture mark his works. He mainly worked in Vicenza, and also in Venice, Verona and Padua. Giovanni Bellini influenced him heavily, and he might have worked in Bellini's workshop around 1470. His son Benedetto was a productive engraver. Vasari says he was a student of Mantegna. He died in 1523.

Edward Bierstadt took portrait and landscape photographs, worked as an engraver, and was a pioneer of color photography in the United States. His father was a cooper in Solingen, and the family moved to New Bedford, Massachusetts, when he was a boy. His younger brother was the noted painter Albert Bierstadt. In 1860 he opened a studio in New York City with Albert.

Xiang Shengmo came from Xiushui, now Jiaxing in Zhejiang, and was the grandson of the great painting collector Xiang Yuanbian. His courtesy name was Kongzhang and his art names were Yi'an and Xushan Qiao. His painting followed the style of Wen Zhengming. Landscapes and flowers, with an elegant taste, were his specialty. He lived in the Ming dynasty. Dates: 1597 to 1658.

A royal upholsterer fathered Gabriel François Doyen, and he first opposed his son's wish to become an artist. At twelve Gabriel began taking lessons from Charles-André van Loo. He made rapid progress and won the Grand Prix de Rome at twenty. In 1748 he set out for Italy, and in 1752 he joined the Academy of France in Rome. Historical and mythological scenes were his subjects. He died in 1806.

A prosperous jeweler fathered Léon Frédéric. In 1871 the boy was apprenticed to the architect and decorative painter Charle-Albert and began night courses at the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels. Three years later he found a place in the workshop of Jean-François Portaels. His earliest paintings joined Christian mysticism with pantheistic themes, and later works increasingly reflected social concerns. Flemish art of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries also shows in his work.

Salomon Gessner is best known as a poet, for his Idylls. He also painted, made graphic art and served as a government official. He co-founded the Helvetic Society and was the first publisher and editor of the Neue Zürcher Zeitung. His father was a printer and publisher on the High Council of Zürich. A bookshop apprenticeship in Berlin in 1749 lasted only a year. Art was his choice.

Money was tight for Claude Ferdinand Gaillard, who at first had to engrave fashion plates to make a living. His chief master was Léon Cogniet, with whom he began engraving in 1850, the year he entered the École des Beaux-Arts. His application to his art brought him the Prix de Rome for engraving in 1856. At his first public showing in 1860, his prints were called laboured, soft and flaccid. He was born and died in Paris.

Nothing is known of Hans Eworth's early life or training. Recorded as Jan Euworts, he was a freeman of the Guild of St Luke in Antwerp in 1540. With other exiled Flemings he made a career in Tudor London, painting allegorical images and portraits of the gentry and nobility. About 40 paintings are now attributed to him, among them portraits of Mary I and Elizabeth I. In the early 1570s he did decorative work for Elizabeth's Office of the Revels.

Pinturicchio got his nickname, little painter, because of his small stature, and he used it to sign some of his works. His real name was Bernardino di Betto, and he came from Perugia. He may have trained under lesser-known Perugian painters such as Bonfigli and Fiorenzo di Lorenzo. He worked in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. He also went by Benetto di Biagio or Sordicchio. He died in 1513.

Vigilius Eriksen studied first under Johann Salomon Wahl. He won a gold medal at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts but was denied entry into the institution. He quickly got a name for his portraits, and from 1757 to 1772 he traveled and worked in Saint Petersburg, where he became imperial court painter. He painted several portraits of Catherine the Great and other royals. He was the royal portraitist to Christian VI of Denmark.

Adolf Hirémy-Hirschl painted historical and mythological subjects, particularly of ancient Rome. He came from a Jewish family in Temesvár, then part of Hungary. Some of his major history paintings have been lost, and his heirs kept many smaller works until the early 1980s. Though he was one of the most successful artists in fin-de-siècle Vienna, the rise of Gustav Klimt and the Secessionists put his reputation in eclipse.

Born in Bologna, Francesco Primaticcio trained under Giulio Romano in Mantua and became a pupil of Innocenzo da Imola, making decorations at the Palazzo Te. In 1532 he took a position at the court of Francis I of France. With Rosso Fiorentino he was one of the leading artists at the Château de Fontainebleau, in the so-called First School of Fontainebleau, and he spent much of his life there. He worked as a painter, architect and sculptor.

Joseph Henry Sharp is considered the Spiritual Father of the Taos Society of Artists, which he helped found. He was one of the earliest European-American artists to visit Taos, New Mexico, which he first saw in 1893 with John Hauser. He painted American Indian portraits and cultural life, as well as Western landscapes. Theodore Roosevelt commissioned him to paint portraits of 200 Native American warriors who survived the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

The Wild Hunt of Odin is the best known work of Peter Nicolai Arbo, and he painted it in two versions, now in Stockholm and Oslo. It shows a female figure from Norse mythology. Arbo grew up at Gulskogen Manor in Drammen, the son of a headmaster. He specialized in portraits and large narrative scenes from Norwegian history and Norse mythology. He lived from 1831 to 1892.

Guillaume Philippe Benoist engraved some portraits and a few other subjects. He came from near Coutances in Normandy and spent the later part of his life in London, where he died. Joseph Strutt wrote in the late 18th century that he chiefly confined himself to small plates, which he executed in a fine style, though with little taste. Among his portraits is one of Galileo after F. Villamena. He lived from 1725 to 1770.

Stefano da Verona, also called Stefano da Zevio, was the son of the French painter Jean d'Arbois, who came to Italy to the court of Gian Galeazzo Visconti. He likely apprenticed at Pavia with illuminators of the Visconti. Michelino da Besozzo influenced him, as the Madonna of the Rose Garden shows. Before settling in Verona he worked at Padua. In Verona he made his major works. He was active there until about 1438.

Karel van Mander is mainly remembered for his Schilder-boeck, a biography of Early Netherlandish painters and Northern Renaissance artists. He was also a painter, playwright, poet and art theorist. He came from Flanders and settled in the Dutch Republic in the latter part of his life. As an artist and art theorist he played a significant role in the spread of Northern Mannerism there. He lived from 1548 to 1606.

Michael Burghers was baptised in a Lutheran church in Amsterdam and apprenticed as an engraver. He settled in England when Louis XIV took Utrecht, in 1672. Probably in early 1673 he arrived in Oxford, where he became David Loggan's assistant. English aristocrats commissioned maps, estate plans and illustrations of stately houses from him. He spent most of his career in England as an illustrator. He died in 1727.

The first reliable reference to Watanabe Shikō is a diary of the Konoe family from 1708. From that entry it may be inferred that he was a rōnin in the employ of Konoe Iehiro. A notebook kept by a samurai doctor, Yamashina Dōan, also mentions him. He painted in the Rinpa school and was also known as Motooki or Kyūma. His other art names included Shōken and Soshin. He died in 1755.

A pupil of Pieter Coecke van Aelst in Antwerp in 1529, Willem Key later took lessons together with Frans Floris from Lambert Lombardus in Liège. He became a member of the Guild of St Luke in Antwerp in 1540. He was a rich man and lived in a large house in the center of town near the exchange. He married Johanna Reyns. His daughter Susanna married a painter. He came from Breda and died in 1568.

William Brymner played an important part in the development of Impressionism in Canada, and he taught numerous artists who became leading figures in Canadian modern art. He was the son of Douglas Brymner, the first Dominion Archivist. His family moved from Scotland to Canada East when he was a toddler, then to Montreal, and later to the Ottawa area. There he attended the Ottawa Grammar School. He began with architectural studies.

Andrea Vanni was active mainly in Siena, where he was born around 1332. The first notice of him as a painter comes from 1353, when he was associated with Bartolo di Fredi, though it is uncertain if he was a painter or an assistant. His last activity dates to about 1400. He also helped found the new government of Siena and held several offices for twenty years.

Anson Dickinson painted miniature portraits and became famous during his lifetime for a very large number of works, though he is now largely forgotten. He was the oldest of ten children, born in Milton, a district of Litchfield, Connecticut. His father was a master carpenter. For a while he was apprenticed to a silversmith in Litchfield. He did enamel work, made frames and painted signs. He lived from 1779 to 1852.

First apprenticed as a shoemaker to his father, Carl Hasenpflug then trained with the decorative painter Carl Gropius in Berlin. By 1822 he was known as a painter of architectural subjects, especially medieval German churches. He drew architectural details first in pen, then glazed over them with oil paint. Favorite subjects included the cathedrals of Magdeburg and Halberstadt, where he lived from 1828. He died in 1858.

In the late 1800s Helga Marie Ring Reusch travelled to France, Spain, Italy and the United States. She came from Fredrikstad and studied with Erik Werenskiold, Hans Heyerdahl, Eilif Peterssen and Gerhard Munthe. She married the geologist Hans Henrik Reusch. She exhibited often at the Høstutstillingen, and her work was shown at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893. She lived from 1865 to 1944.

John Linton Chapman moved with his family to Rome, where he and his brother Conrad studied art under their father, John Gadsby Chapman. There he painted Italian peasants, scenes and landscapes. He was described as talented but also lazy and unambitious, and he made a living selling repeated versions of the same works. He returned to the United States in 1878 and lived in poverty. He worked as a painter and photographer.

Pietro Bettelini began studying art at a young age in Caslano. He had instruction from Gandolfi and Bartolozzi, but his later works lean toward the style of Raphael Morghen. Thorvaldsen held him in high esteem and employed him to engrave some of his finest works, both figures and reliefs. His Entombment after Andrea del Sarto, in the Florence Gallery, is among his finest. Swiss engraver. He died at Rome.

Amélie Lundahl was the youngest of eleven children in Oulu. Her mother died when she was three months old, and her father, a town prosecutor, died when she was eight. From 1872 to 1876 she studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Helsinki, with a short stay at the School of Art and Design in Stockholm, made possible by a travel grant. Another grant took her to Paris.

Francis Tattegrain became famous for pictures of fishermen's life on the northern French coast, and he led the École de Berck. He came from a family with a long legal tradition. His father, President of the Court of Amiens, let him study painting on the promise that he would also study law. He did, and earned a doctorate. His interest in art began in 1865. He died in Arras in 1915.

Francisco Domingo Marqués started in Valencia at the Real Academia de San Carlos, under Rafael Montesinos, a great admirer of Ribera. Domingo copied Ribera's works as his first exercises. In 1864 he moved to Madrid to continue at the Real Academia de San Fernando with Federico de Madrazo. Three years later he won a pension. He painted in an Eclectic style and died in 1920.

John F. Francis taught himself art, mostly, and worked as a portrait painter in central and eastern Pennsylvania until 1845. His portraits show an early fascination with minute detail. In 1845 he began exhibiting at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and the Philadelphia Art Union. Later he turned to still lifes. He came from Philadelphia and died in 1886.

King Manuel I named Jorge Afonso royal painter in 1508, and King John III did so again in 1529. He was based mainly in Lisbon, with a workshop near the Igreja de São Domingos. A whole generation of Portuguese painters trained there, among them Cristóvão de Figueiredo, Garcia Fernandes and Gregório Lopes. Old Queen Leonor commissioned his main altarpieces. He died in 1540.

Peter Gertner received citizenship of Nuremberg on 12 January 1521, and he presumably learned from the painter Wolf Traut. He became known as a portrait painter and worked for Casimir, Margrave of Brandenburg-Kulmbach, in 1527. After Casimir's widow Susanna of Bavaria remarried, Peter went with her to the court of Neuburg an der Donau. There he worked as Master Peter, Court Painter.

Detailed and accurate portraits of ships under sail made William Anderson well regarded. He showed them in London every year between 1787 and 1811, and occasionally until 1834. His early life is obscure, but he trained as a shipwright and moved to London to become a maritime painter at about thirty. He influenced John Ward and others of the Hull school. He was Scottish.

Anna Rosina de Gasc was born Lisiewska into a family of painters of Polish noble origin in Berlin. Her father Georg taught painting to her and her siblings Anna Dorothea and Christoph Friedrich. She later studied with Antoine Pesne and learned his style. She mostly painted portraits. Her portraits include one of Johanna Charlotte of Anhalt. She lived from 1713 to 1783.

Eric Ravilious grew up in Sussex and is known particularly for his watercolours of the South Downs and Castle Hedingham. They examine English landscape and vernacular art with an off-kilter, modernist clarity. He also designed and illustrated books and made wood-engravings. He served as a war artist. When the aircraft he was in was lost off Iceland in 1942, he became the first British war artist to die on active service in World War II.

Hendrick de Clerck worked in Brussels in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. He belongs stylistically to the late Mannerist generation before Rubens and the Flemish Baroque. His paintings are like those of Maerten de Vos, who was thirty years older, though not as powerful. He was court painter to the Governors General of the Spanish Netherlands. His date of birth is not known. He died in 1630.

James Frothingham started as a chaise painter in his father's chaise factory in Charlestown, Massachusetts. In the Boston area he studied with Gilbert Stuart. An 1888 Atlantic Monthly called him a portraitist of talent, and quoted Stuart as saying of one of his heads that no man in Boston but himself could paint so good a head. He painted portraits in Massachusetts and New York. His daughter Sarah was a painter too.

A sculptor, Franz Anton von Zauner, recognized Leopold Kupelwieser's talent early, and by twelve the boy was already attending the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. His father co-owned a factory that produced tableware. During a stay in Rome in 1824 he came under the influence of the Nazarene movement. He painted portraits of Archduke Johann and the Lössl family. He lived from 1796 to 1862.

Luca Penni was nicknamed Le Romain, the Roman, though he was born in Florence into a family of weavers. His brothers Gianfrancesco and Bartolommeo were also painters. He seems to have trained under Raphael. In the late 1520s he worked in Genoa with his brother-in-law Perino del Vaga. He is best known for his work in France as part of the First School of Fontainebleau, alongside Rosso Fiorentino.

Nobody knows who the Master of Hoogstraeten was. The name is a Notname given to a Flemish painter, or a group of painters, active in Antwerp in the early 16th century. The master made mostly religious paintings and is counted among the Antwerp Mannerists. Some have tried to link him with Passchier van der Mersch, a pupil of Hans Memling. A clear Dutch influence in his work has also been noted.

William Rothenstein's subjects ranged from landscapes in France to Jewish synagogues in London. He is perhaps best known as a war artist in both world wars, for his portraits, and for his popular memoirs of the 1930s. More than two hundred of his portraits of famous people are in the National Portrait Gallery. The Tate also holds a large collection of his work. He wrote and lectured on art as well.

Alfred Basel's father owned a factory in Vienna. He studied at the Kunstgewerbeschule under Felician von Myrbach from 1892 to 1898. In the First World War he was a reserve officer, serving with the Fourth Army on the Galician front from March 1915. That fall he fell ill and was declared unfit. By November he was a war artist with the Kriegspressequartier. He painted and etched.

Antonín Hudeček came from Ředhošť in Bohemia. After primary school in Roudnice he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Prague, with Maximilian Pirner and Václav Brožík, devoting himself mostly to figure painting. He continued in Munich with Otto Seitz and opened a workshop in Prague in 1895. Shortly after he joined a group of painters. He became a Czech landscape painter and died in 1941.

His name appears as La Montagne, Montagne and Montaigne, but Nicolas de Plattemontagne was born Nicolas van Plattenberg, in Paris. His father Matthieu was a Flemish painter and engraver from Antwerp who specialized in maritime scenes. His uncle, the engraver Jean Morin, gave him his first lessons in engraving. In his youth he studied with Philippe de Champaigne. He painted and engraved. He died in 1706.

Taddeo Gaddi, born in Florence, was the son of the painter Gaddo Gaddi. He belonged to Giotto's workshop from 1313 until the master's death in 1337. Vasari considered him Giotto's most talented pupil, and in 1347 he was placed at the top of a list of Florence's best painters. He also traded as a merchant with a branch in Venice. He worked as a mosaicist and architect too.

Antonio Zanchi trained in Venice with Giacomo Pedrali, Matteo Ponzone and Francesco Ruschi. He etched the frontispieces for several opera librettos in his younger years. He painted prolifically in the Baroque style. Most of his work is in Venice. It can also be seen in Padua, Verona, Vicenza, Brescia, Milan and Bavaria. He was born in Este in 1631.

Melbourne is where Frederick McCubbin was born and raised. He studied at the National Gallery of Victoria Art School under Eugene von Guerard and later George Folingsby. One of his classmates, Tom Roberts, returned from art training in Europe in 1885, and that summer the two set up the Box Hill artists' camp. McCubbin was a prominent member of the Heidelberg School, also called Australian impressionism. He taught art too.

Heinrich Lefler's father was the painter Franz Lefler. He studied at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna under Christian Griepenkerl, and then in Munich with Nikolaus Gysis and Wilhelm von Diez. In 1900 he was a founding member of the Hagenbund. For three years he assisted Anton Brioschi, the head designer at the court theatre. He worked as a painter, graphic artist and stage designer. He lived from 1863 to 1919.

George Barret Sr. left Ireland to make his name in London, and he quickly became a leading artist of the period. He painted landscapes in oil and watercolour. He exhibited at the Society of Artists of Great Britain and won patronage from many leading art collectors. In 1768 he left the Society with other leading members to found the Royal Academy, where he exhibited until 1782. He died in 1784.

Chelsea is where Walter Greaves grew up, the son of a boat builder and waterman who had been J. M. W. Turner's boatman. In 1863 Walter and his brother Henry met James McNeill Whistler and introduced him to the sights of the Thames. They became Whistler's studio assistants and close friends for over twenty years. Walter painted, etched and drew topographical views. He died in 1930.

Ships fascinated Carl Locher from an early age, and his first training came from his father, who painted ship portraits for a living. When his father died, he carried on the business for a short while and sailed on several voyages. He was born in Flensburg, then part of Denmark. He became a Danish realist painter and an early member of the Skagen group. He lived from 1851 to 1915.

Edward Okuń came from a noble family and was orphaned early, growing up with his maternal grandparents. After inheriting a large fortune, he soon took drawing lessons from great painters. He painted landscapes and portraits, designed covers and illustrated magazines, including the German Jugend. In his younger years he also raced as a cyclist in the Kingdom of Poland. He was a freemason and an Art Nouveau painter. He lived from 1872 to 1945.

Eva Bonnier came from a leading family of publishers in Stockholm, and her father was the publisher Albert Bonnier. She studied painting with August Malmström and joined the women's section of the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts in 1878. With her friend Hanna Hirsch she travelled to Paris in 1883 and stayed there until 1889. Her painting Music dates from that year. She was also a philanthropist.

Frans Luycx became the leading portrait painter at the imperial court of Emperor Ferdinand III in Vienna. He is best known for portraits of the Emperor's family and various members of the Habsburgs, including the Austrian and Spanish branches. He was baptized in Antwerp Cathedral in 1604, the son of a silk cloth merchant. He was a Flemish painter. He died in 1668.

Rueland Frueauf the Elder lived and worked most of his life in Obernberg am Inn. He mostly painted frescoes in local churches. In 1484 he was appointed a consultant to work with Michael Pacher on an altarpiece for the Franciscan Order. His son Rueland the Younger also became a painter. He died in Passau in 1507. He painted in the Late Gothic style.

Louis Royer received many commissions from the Dutch royal family and for public statues. He first studied at the academy in his native Mechelen, and later in the studio of Jan Frans van Geel. After a year of study in Paris he went to live in Amsterdam in 1820. He was a Flemish sculptor who worked in the Netherlands. He lived from 1793 to 1868.

William Holbrook Beard is best known for satirical paintings of beasts performing human-like activities. He came from Painesville, Ohio, studied abroad, and has links to the Düsseldorf school. In 1861 he moved to New York City, and a year later he became a member of the National Academy of Design. He opened his own studio in the Tenth Street Studio Building. He died in 1900.

Ludwig Passini's father was the engraver Johann Nepomuk Passini, and the family moved from Vienna to Trieste in 1850. In 1864 Ludwig married Anna Warschauer, who was a great-granddaughter of the banker Joseph Mendelssohn. She died two years later. He painted narrative and genre scenes and made prints. He is also called Ludovico Passini. He lived from 1832 to 1903.

Patrick Nasmyth was one of eleven children, the eldest son of the artist Alexander Nasmyth of Edinburgh. He was named after his father's patron, Patrick Miller. His six sisters were notable artists, and his younger brother James was an engineer who invented the steam hammer. Patrick painted landscapes in Scotland and England. He was Scottish. He lived from 1787 to 1831.

A pupil of Charles Le Brun, René-Antoine Houasse worked under his direction at the Gobelins manufactory and on the decoration of Versailles. He directed the French Academy in Rome for five years. He painted a whole series of pictures on myths about the goddess Athena or Minerva. In 1673 he married Marie Le Blé, a cousin of Le Brun. He died in 1710.

Ventura Salimbeni was born Ventura di Arcangelo Salimbeni, and he was later also called Bevilacqua. He painted in the Counter-Maniera manner and made prints. Vaghezza and sensual refinement strongly influenced him. He lived from 1568 to 1613.
